summary: Three hostile judges attack the "focus mode for groceries" purpose-bound card idea, then a defender rebuilds it

verdicts.strongest_objection: The headline part, a card that only works for your groceries, is already a paid feature you can buy today. Privacy.com sells "Groceries" category cards that decline at non-grocery merchants. Greenlight, Kit and True Link block merchants and categories, CardControl pitches category locks as a way to stop impulse clothing buys, Fluz sells MCC category locks, and Kando issues a virtual card scoped to one errand. The only step past those, a card that buys only what is on your list, depends on item-level declines, and those do not exist at a physical register. This team already lost that fight once. Round 1 killed Listcard/Slip on exactly this premise, so a judge would see the same mocked "not on your list" decline at checkout as before. Without the item-level claim, Focus card is a Privacy.com category card with a weekly cap. The other two parts are also covered. Ad-free online shopping ships as Amazon extensions (ShopSuey, De-Sponsor, Banish Amazon Sponsored, Amazon Sponsored Product Blocker), and Ruko is a Chrome extension that blurs purchase buttons but lets you whitelist groceries. The 'swipe Tinder-style between options for your list' idea is Devpost 'Store Run'. The agent-checkout path runs straight into Walmart and Amazon limiting outside agents. The diminished-reality lens is the only part with no shipped consumer product, but it is published research and patented, so judges who know AR will not see the blur effect itself as new. Taken together, this is three existing things bundled, not one new thing.

Greenlight merchant/category blocks: https://help.greenlight.com/hc/en-us/articles/47951314307227-How-do-I-block-a-store-or-merchant. verdicts.which_part_is_strongest: The lens is the only part that carries the idea. At the expo table, 18 snacks blurring and 2 glowing is visually striking. It runs on Perceptron's grounding and counting, and no consumer product ships it; prior art there is CHI and UvA research and patents only. Cut the card as the headline, because it is Privacy.com's Groceries card and its item-level decline is the same mock that got Listcard and Slip killed. Cut the feed entirely, because it is a weaker bundle of Amazon ad-blocker extensions, Ruko and a Store Run-style swipe UI. It also depends on agent access that Walmart and Amazon are actively shutting down.
verdicts.fix: Rebuild around the lens and make Visa the consequence of what the camera sees, not an item-level decline. (1) Lens: blur the items not on the list, as now. (2) The camera reads the shelf tag for each list item and places a sandbox hold for the sum. The card cap is that number and nothing more, which is a real Visa amount control. (3) When the camera sees an off-list item go into the basket, it doesn't fake a register decline. It fires a Payment Instructions-style approval prompt to a friend, or to a 'future you' with a 10-minute cool-off, before the cap goes up for that item's tag price. Declining leaves the cap where it is, so the register refuses the higher total. That is a real amount-level decline with an honest story. (4) Partial-capture to the receipt and void the rest of the hold. Present it as list-sized money plus a lens, never as 'a card that knows SKUs'. Say plainly that ShoppingCoach exists and that this differs in using your own list instead of a nutrition score, and in being tied to real money. If the team can't make the approval moment fun for a 20-year-old, move to another concept.

verdicts.strongest_objection: Every part of this is something I'd have to choose to put up with, and I can opt out of all of it whenever I want, so it feels like a parent I hired myself. The card only works if I take my normal debit card out of my wallet, and the moment I want Takis I tap the other card. A self-control lock that I hold the key to is just a settings screen with extra steps. Holding my phone up in the Trader Joe's snack aisle so it can blur the snacks is the most embarrassing thing I could do in that store. I already know where the oat milk is, and the impulse buy happens at the register, not while I'm scanning shelves. The 'not on your list' moment in the 10-second demo is also faked. You told us yourselves that a real register can't decline one item, so the punchline a Visa judge will poke at is the mocked part. The feed is an ad blocker for Instacart. I'd install that as a free extension, and nobody gives it a second thought. Whether I'd tell my roommate about it tonight: no. 'I made my card stop me from buying chips' is something you confess, not something you recommend.
verdicts.prior_art: This team's own round 1 already ran the card: Listcard ('a card that can only buy what's written on it') was rebuilt as Slip and then killed. The reasons were that item-level enforcement is mocked and that the restriction duplicates Privacy.com, Kando Errands and Greenlight. The batch diagnosis said outright to drop SKU enforcement and utility/friction pitches. Purpose-bound cards already exist: SNAP/EBT and FSA cards use IIAS item filtering, Greenlight and BusyKid have parent-locked category cards, and Privacy.com offers merchant-locked caps. On the self-control side there are budgeting and lock apps like YNAB, Opal, one sec and Freedom, plus Studuvalley in the winners list ('break the cycle of brainrot'), which is the same anti-temptation pitch. The lens has real-world ad-removing diminished reality precedent in Brand Killer, a 2015 hackathon project that blurred logos through a headset, and in academic DR ad-blocking demos. The feed has precedent in browser extensions and uBlock filter lists that strip Amazon/Instacart sponsored results. Agent checkout over TAP is now the standard Visa-track move. Taken alone, none of the three parts is new.
verdicts.which_part_is_strongest: The lens carries the idea. 18 snacks blurring while 2 glow is the only moment a judge feels in their hands, and Perceptron grounding and counting can actually do it on a demo shelf. Cut the card first. It is the most mocked part (no in-store item declines), it repeats the already-killed Listcard/Slip, and it is where the parent-and-homework feeling comes from. Cut the feed second, because it is a sponsored-slot blocker with a Tinder skin, and the agent-checkout part is filler. One problem stays even if you keep the lens: it carries the demo but has no real use case for discipline, since students won't hold up a phone to be told no.
verdicts.fix: Kill the Focus framing. If the team wants to keep anything, turn the lens from restriction into speed and money for the user: point the phone at the shelf and see which item is cheapest per ounce, or where your list items are, or which item a roommate already bought. That gives the user an edge instead of a scolding, and a student would actually raise a phone to save $2. The Visa role then has to be a real sandbox control triggered by what the camera sees, such as a hold that partial-captures to the real price, rather than an item decline at a register, which can't be done. The more honest call is to go back to the round 1 batch diagnosis: pick a food moment that isn't a grocery errand, use a physical prop the judge acts on, and make money moving the fun payoff. Self-imposed restriction on ordinary groceries fails the 'would a 20-year-old do this unprompted on a Friday' test, and no change to the interface fixes that.

verdicts.strongest_objection:
The pitch's own 10-second demo ends with "checkout says 'not on your list'" for a snack grabbed off a physical shelf. That is a mocked item-level decline at an in-person register, which is the exact thing the brief says can't be done today. Take that beat out and the part I can touch, the lens, has nothing to do with Visa. Blurring products is a computer-vision trick, and the card is added on afterward. The only part that is both real and tied to Visa is the online feed, and that runs on an agent shopping for you through TAP checkout, which is an agent-at-the-core pattern I'd also kill. So each of the three parts fails a different rule: the card needs a fake decline, the lens is unrelated to Visa, and the feed puts an agent at the core.

The Visa-unease question settles it. Self-control on its own is fine, because Visa sells controls and trust: caps, Payment Instructions mandates, token suspend. But this pitch is framed as anti-ads, smaller baskets and "the store is your enemy." Retailers are Visa's acquiring-side customers, retail media is something Visa is actively courting, and Visa earns on volume. A Visa judge would hear "we cut merchant revenue and shrink transactions." I'd smile and score someone else. Two more problems: Instacart and Walmart already let you filter or hide promoted items, and sponsored-slot hiders already exist as browser extensions, so "incumbents can't" is weaker than it sounds. And building live per-product blur plus hand-to-basket tracking on 20 SKUs in 36 hours is possible, but it uses up the whole build on the part that has no Visa in it.
verdicts.prior_art: The team's own round 1 work already covered this. Listcard ("your grocery list is the card, can only buy what's written on it") is the Focus card under a new name, and the round 1 executioner rejected the whole cluster of scoped grocery cards that depend on item-level enforcement. Banter Mart (on the DubHacks winners list as "Humans swipe, agents type") already did swipe-to-shop plus agents, which is the Focus feed. Purpose-bound credentials already exist: FSA/HSA and SNAP cards enforced through IIAS, Greenlight and other kid cards with merchant locks, and Privacy.com merchant-locked virtual cards. Ad-free grocery browsing already exists too: browser extensions that hide Instacart and Amazon sponsored listings, and retailer filters for promoted items. The lens (diminished reality, highlighting only your list items) has been shown in AR shopping-list research and in retailer AR wayfinding features. The one fresh element is blurring things out instead of highlighting things in. That is a nice inversion, but it's only one feature.
verdicts.which_part_is_strongest: The lens carries the idea. When the judge holds up the phone, 18 products blur and 2 glow, and that is a real first-10-second moment with the judge as the actor. It is the only part with a wow. Cut the feed completely: it's agent buying, it can't be touched at a table, and Banter Mart already did it. Shrink the card to the Visa controls that actually run in the sandbox: a hold equal to the list total, a merchant and expiry lock, partial capture or void. Drop the claim that the card "can only be used for that item," because in a store that is impossible without faking it. The problem: once you cut it down that far, there's no Visa story left that I'd reward, so the lens is a CV demo looking for a payment reason.
verdicts.fix:
If the team insists on keeping it, rebuild around the lens and make the payment consequence real and visible, without faking an item decline.

(1) Start a trip: the app places a real Cybersource sandbox hold equal to the priced list total plus a small buffer, under a Payment Instructions-style mandate (this store, 90-minute expiry).

(2) When the camera sees you pick up a blurred item, it doesn't decline anything. It fires the mandate's real approval prompt or step-up: "$4.29 Takis is off-list. Raise your cap?" The prompt goes to you, or to an accountability buddy's phone, which makes it two-sided and gives the judge a second actor. Approving raises the hold. Ignoring it leaves the cap where it was, so the real register auth for the full cart amount will decline if you exceed it. Amount caps at a register are real. Item caps are not.

(3) At the end, receipt OCR partially captures the hold and voids the remainder. The table shows "you saved $11.40 versus your usual trip."

(4) Pitch it as trust and control for the cardholder ("Visa gives you the guardrails you choose"), not as anti-ads or anti-merchant. Present it as an issuer or bank feature and drop the "Instacart can't do this" line.

Even rebuilt, it's a 5 at best. The camera-blur moment and the Visa moment are still two separate things joined by a prompt. My recommendation is to keep the blur-the-shelf visual as a demo technique, put it in an idea where the camera's verdict moves money as the punchline, and drop the self-control-against-merchants framing.

rebuilt.one_sentence: Point your phone at a shelf and everything fades except what you came for and the treats your budget can still cover; the card's limit for this trip is set to exactly that amount, a real Visa hold priced by the camera.
rebuilt.what_got_cut:
All three judges killed the original idea with scores of 4, 3 and 3. All three agreed the lens is the only part worth keeping. Here is what goes:

1. THE FEED IS GONE. That means no agent shopping, no TAP signed checkout, no ad-free Instacart layer and no Tinder swipe. It reruns Banter Mart, Store Run and the Amazon sponsored-result blockers (ShopSuey, De-Sponsor). It puts an agent at the core, which the expo judge kills on sight. It also depends on agent access that Walmart and Amazon are shutting down.

2. THE CARD IS NO LONGER THE HEADLINE, AND THE ITEM-LEVEL CLAIM IS DROPPED. We never say "a card that only buys what's on your list." Item-level declines at a physical register don't exist, and Listcard/Slip already died in round 1 on that exact mock. On its own the card is Privacy.com's Groceries category card. What's left is a short-lived token locked to one merchant, with a dollar cap.

3. THE ANTI-ADS / ANTI-MERCHANT PITCH IS GONE. That includes "Instacart can't do this because of ad revenue" and "the store is your enemy." Retailers are Visa's acquiring-side customers, so that framing puts a Visa judge off. We pitch it as cardholder control: "Visa gives you the guardrails you choose."

4. THE FAKE DEMO ENDING IS GONE. Checkout no longer says "not on your list." Every decline in the demo is a real amount-level decline from a sandbox auth.

5. THE "PARENT YOU HIRED" FRAMING IS GONE. The lens is no longer a scold. It shows what you're allowed (the treat slot glows gold), not just what you aren't.
rebuilt.the_new_thing:
Two things change, and both make the camera's verdict move real money. The card is no longer a passive restriction.

1. THE CAMERA PRICES YOUR LIST AND SETS THE HOLD. When you start a trip, the lens grounds each list item on the shelf with Perceptron, reads its shelf tag (OCR) and adds up the real prices. It adds your treat slot (say $5), then places a real sandbox authorization hold for exactly that amount on a single-use trip token. The token is locked to this merchant and expires in 90 minutes, under a Payment Instructions-style mandate. Nobody types in the cap; the shelf sets it. Privacy.com makes you guess a limit. This one is priced from what the camera reads.

2. A TREAT-SLOT LENS INSTEAD OF A BLUR-EVERYTHING LENS. List items glow green. Off-list items that still fit your remaining treat money glow gold ("you can have this"). Everything else fades. When you pick up a gold item (it fills the center of the frame for about 1 second, with tap as a fallback), the treat meter drops live. The gold set shrinks right away, because fewer things are affordable now. If you pick up a faded item, an approval prompt goes to your buddy (a roommate or the person you shop with): "Anson wants Takis, $4.29. Allow / Deny." Allow sends a real incremental auth that raises the hold. Deny leaves the cap where it is, so at checkout the auth for the full basket declines on amount, honestly. After checkout we partial-capture the receipt total, void the rest and suspend the token. Treat money you didn't spend rolls into next week's slot, so the payoff is a growing treat budget, not just "no."

We say openly that ShoppingCoach (CHI EA '24) and US patent 10553032 cover the diminished-reality idea. Our difference: the filter comes from your own list plus a live budget, not a nutrition score, and what the lens sees drives a real Visa hold, incremental auth, capture and void.
rebuilt.demo_script_90s:
PROPS: a tabletop "shelf" with about 20 real snacks, each with a printed price tag. A small basket. A laptop labeled "Register" that runs a sandbox auth for whatever is in the basket. A second phone for the buddy, handed to the judge's partner or a teammate.

0:00-0:10 (judge acts right away): Hand the judge the phone. "Your list is oat milk and granola, and you've got a $5 treat slot. Point it at the shelf." About 17 items fade, 2 glow green and 3 glow gold.

0:10-0:25: "It just read the price tags on your two items: $4.49 plus $5.99, plus $5 of treats. That's a real Visa hold for $15.48 on a one-trip card that only works at this store for 90 minutes." Turn the laptop to show the live sandbox auth response with the amount, the merchant lock and the expiry.

0:25-0:40: "Grab a treat." The judge picks up a gold item (a $2.99 candy bar). The treat meter drops to $2.01 and one gold item fades on the spot, because it's no longer affordable. "Your lens just changed because your money changed."

0:40-0:60: "Now grab the Takis." They're faded. The judge picks them up anyway. The buddy phone buzzes: "Wants Takis, $4.29. Allow / Deny." Let the partner choose. If Deny: "Fine, keep them in the basket and check out." The judge carries the basket to the Register laptop, which runs the auth for the basket total, and it is DECLINED on amount. Say it plainly: "That's a real amount decline. Visa can't refuse one item at a register, and we don't pretend it can. The cap just ends where your plan ends." If Allow: the incremental auth shows the hold rising by $4.29, and checkout approves.

0:60-0:80: Checkout approves on the second pass, with the Takis put back or approved. Show partial capture to the receipt, void of the remaining hold and the trip token suspended. The screen reads: "$2.01 treat money rolls into next week. Next week's slot: $7.01."

0:80-0:90: "Visa already sells purpose-bound money for benefits. We point it at you: a camera that shows only your plan, and a card that's exactly as big as your plan. Guardrails you choose, built only on controls that run in the Visa sandbox today."
rebuilt.visa_role:
REAL IN SANDBOX:
(1) A single-use trip token or virtual credential under a Payment Instructions-style mandate: merchant-locked, 90-minute expiry, with an amount cap equal to the camera-priced list plus the treat slot.
(2) A Cybersource sandbox authorization hold for that cap.
(3) An incremental authorization when the buddy approves an off-list item. The approval prompt is the mandate's step-up.
(4) An amount-level decline when the basket total goes over the cap.
(5) Partial capture to the receipt total, void of the remaining hold, then token suspend (VTS sandbox lifecycle) when the trip ends.

SIMULATED, AND SAID OUT LOUD AT THE TABLE:
(a) The "register" is our laptop sending the auth that a POS would send. It is not a real terminal.
(b) In real life this only binds if you pay with the trip token, for example through Apple Pay. Nothing stops you from tapping a different card.
(c) We never claim item-level enforcement. All enforcement is amount-based. The camera decides how big the amount is, and Visa enforces it.

PITCH FRAME: an issuer or bank feature that grows card usage among students ("Visa gives you guardrails you choose"). It is not anti-merchant and not anti-ads. The merchant still gets the sale, captured in full.
rebuilt.why_students_use_it:
Honestly, this is the weakest part. Best case:

(1) The treat slot changes the feeling from "my app says no" to "my app tells me what I can have guilt-free." Rollover gives a visible streak that grows, so restraint feels like earning money, not losing it.

(2) Speed in an unfamiliar store. The glow finds the exact oat milk your roommate wants in two seconds. That's a reason to raise the phone that isn't about discipline.

(3) The buddy prompt is social. Roommates on a shared house budget, or a couple splitting groceries, get an Allow/Deny ping. That's funny and shareable in a way that "I locked my card" isn't.

(4) First-apartment students who are new to budgeting want a cap they didn't have to calculate.

Counterpoint we can't fully fix: the cynical-student judge is right that most 20-year-olds won't do this every week unprompted, and holding up a phone in the snack aisle is mildly embarrassing. Plausible use is occasional ("a broke week," "a shared house run"), not daily.
rebuilt.build_36h:
Team of 4. Build on the existing SwiftUI app in the repo.

PERSON 1, VISION (hours 0-30): Perceptron Mk1 grounding prompted with list item names plus "price tag," returning boxes and OCR'd prices. Between model calls, keep boxes locked to products with on-device tracking (Apple Vision VNTrackObjectRequest) so the overlay doesn't lag. Pick-up detection: a grounded item fills more than 40% of the frame for 1 second. Fallback: tap to select. Tune for 20 fixed SKUs under expo lighting by hour 24, and cache a reference image of each SKU.

PERSON 2, iOS LENS + TRIP UX (hours 0-30): Mask rendering in Core Image (desaturate and blur the frame, then composite back green and gold boxes). Treat meter, list entry, trip start/end, an animated "gold set shrinks" moment, rollover screen.

PERSON 3, VISA BACKEND (hours 0-28): Node or Python service. Cybersource sandbox auth, incremental auth, partial capture, void. VTS sandbox token provision and suspend, or a clearly labeled mock if credentials stall. Mandate object (merchant ID, expiry, cap, approver). A push or websocket to the buddy client. Get the sandbox calls working end to end by hour 12. That is the biggest risk, so it starts first.

PERSON 4, BUDDY + REGISTER + STAGE (hours 0-36): Buddy web app (Allow/Deny, works on any phone). Register laptop page: scan basket barcodes with a USB scanner, or use the price-tag list, then fire the auth and show approved or declined large on screen. Buy and tag the 20-snack shelf, print the price tags, build the shelf, write and rehearse the pitch, record a backup video.

MILESTONES: hour 12, sandbox auth/void working plus raw grounding boxes on device. Hour 20, full trip end to end with ugly UI. Hour 24, feature freeze. Hours 24-32, reliability passes (lighting, glare on tags, a recovery button for when the tracker loses an item). Hours 32-36, run the 90-second demo at least 15 times, finish the backup video, Devpost write-up citing ShoppingCoach and the patent as prior art.
rebuilt.fatal_flaw:
The fixes helped, but they don't save it. Three problems remain.

(1) The Visa link is still thin. Underneath, the card is a merchant-locked virtual card with an amount cap (Privacy.com plus an incremental auth). The only new part is that the camera sets the cap. A sharp Visa judge may say the lens and the payment are two demos joined by a prompt, which the expo judge predicted. Expect a score around 5, maybe 6 if the treat-slot moment lands.

(2) It can't really be enforced, and that undercuts the premise. The student holds the key: they can tap their normal card at the register. Every self-imposed control fails the "would a 20-year-old do this unprompted on a Friday" test from the round-1 batch diagnosis, and no UI fixes that.

(3) The lens isn't new to anyone who knows AR (ShoppingCoach, the UvA work, US patent 10553032, Brand Killer). Its novelty is the budget link, not the blur.

Honest recommendation: build this only if the team is set on the grocery-focus idea. The stronger move is to keep the blur-the-shelf lens as a demo technique and move it into a non-errand food moment where the camera's verdict moving money is the fun punchline, not a guardrail. That is the direction the round-1 diagnosis and all three judges point to.
